Things started shifting at church: I’d be full of energy one week, rewriting sermons at 3 a.m., starting three new Bible studies at once, pacing the pulpit like I had lightning in my veins. Then suddenly, I’d drop everything—mid-sentence, mid-project—chasing a new idea that burned too bright to ignore. I don’t know why, but I keep seeing figures in the sanctuary after hours—people who aren’t there. One looks like a man in an old coat, just standing near the altar. I know he’s not real, but I *see* him.

Words have started tripping in my head—rhyming, spinning. "Grace chases the face in the space"—I don’t know what it means, but it echoes when I pray. I also feel watched. Not spiritually—like someone’s *recording* me. The way a child laughs outside, I wonder if it’s coded for me. My wife says I’ve withdrawn. I don’t feel joy like I used to—not in preaching, not in my family. Sometimes, standing on the balcony, a sudden pull comes—just to jump—not because I want to end it, but the urge *jolts* through me.  

I used to have peace. Now I have voices, visions, and a mind that won’t sit still—even when I’m empty inside.

At first, I felt *incredibly* energized, like God had given me a new mission. I was up at 3 a.m. writing sermons, repainting the church, organizing outreach programs—doing ten things at once. But I could never finish anything. I’d start a letter to a parishioner and jump to rearranging the hymnal, then suddenly feel furious if someone interrupted me, even my wife. 

About eight months ago, I began seeing figures in the sanctuary late at night—shadowy people kneeling in the pews, but no one was there. I also started noticing signs everywhere: a license plate, a bird flying past the window—I was sure they were messages meant only for me. I’d catch myself saying things like “The light will fight the night with might and right!”—it made sense to me then, the way the words echoed. 

Three months ago, that high collapsed. I couldn’t feel anything—not joy, not love, not even guilt. I stood at the pulpit and nothing mattered. Lately, when I’m on the balcony, I get sudden urges to step over the edge, not because I’ve planned it, but because part of me wonders if it would finally stop. And here’s the thing—those visions? They never left, even when I wasn’t manic or depressed. They’ve been there more than two months on their own.

I’ll start three different things at once in the salon, rearranging stations, mixing chemicals, texting five clients at once, but nothing gets finished. Other times, I’m laughing, almost giddy, but it doesn’t last. It’s like my moods are sliding around on their own.

And then there’s the other stuff. I keep feeling things crawling on my skin, like bugs, but when I look—nothing. I’ve brushed my arms in the middle of a trim, trying to shake it off. I sometimes think… the world feels fake, like it’s all going to vanish. Like none of this matters, and it’s all ending soon. I stopped opening the salon for weeks. Didn’t care. I’d stare at the wall, too heavy to move. I even filled a bottle with pills once—didn’t take them, but… I had it ready.

Talking? It’s hard. My thoughts get tangled. I’ll say things and not know how I got there. My staff look at me like I’m speaking another language. I don’t know what’s worse—the buzzing in my head or the silence after.

Then the voices started—wait, not voices. I felt things crawling on my skin, like bugs, but when I looked, nothing was there. Even now, I feel fingers brushing my arms. I became convinced the world was ending—that a storm was coming that would wipe everything out. That feeling stuck, even when my mood crashed three months ago. I stopped opening the salon. Didn’t want to live. I even swallowed a bunch of pills.

But here’s the thing—those manic highs never really left. Even now, with the bugs on my skin and the doom in my head, I still can’t sit still, and my thoughts race. I think he’s been leaving little signs. Notes in the hem of clothes I didn’t sew. He must care. I’d know if he didn’t. I can feel his attention.
